title: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
description: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters i
body: Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during an interview on "The Circuit with Emily Chang" at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, April 30, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAnthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported.The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs."Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

schema.headline: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption

title: Tech stocks had a nice oversold bounce on Monday. Earnings this week will determine if it's for real
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on Oct. 14, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesT
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on Oct. 14, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesThis week's major earnings hold the key to whether this technology comeback has legs, investors said.The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite rallied Monday, largely due to a rebound in artificial intelligence  companies. Chip stocks surged, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) on pace to snap a nine-day slump. The Magnificent Seven outperformed, as did memory chip makers. The iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), dominated by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, surged 4% after also suffering steep declines over the past week. That comes after the S&P 500 fell nearly 2% last week, its worst weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.5% over the same five-day span. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNasdaq Composite, YTDMonday looked like a bounce from oversold conditions, but a bigger move will depend on this week's big tech earnings — which include results from major names such as Meta Platforms and Tesla — to clear some of the recent worries about the sustainability of the AI trade. SpaceX reports after the bell Tuesday."Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration," wrote Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays.This week will be especially crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support so as not to confirm a further breakdown, Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, said in a Monday note. For the time being, however, widespread, short-term oversold conditions suggest support can hold, she said.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconS&P 500, YTDEarnings test Of the 47 S&P 500 companies that have reported their third quarter thus far, 85% have beaten expectations, and the broad market index is on track to post a blended earnings growth rate of 29%.But the bulk of tech results are still to come, and they have a high bar to clear. "Investors are going to need proof statements from any company that is considered part of the AI trade that they can deliver on the earnings growth expectations being built into their pricing," said Ron Albahary, chief investment officer at LNW. "We don't have a valuation-potential bubble here like we had in the internet bubble. We have an earnings-expectation-potential bubble in this cycle."As a result, the market will take a "more discriminating" approach to tech, which Albahary views as a healthy move that will lead to "more of a dispersion of winners and losers within the AI trade universe." In that environment, some AI beneficiaries may continue to rise, while others like the neocloud platforms may sell off due to the amount of debt they're taking on to finance the build-out, he said. "Previously, the AI headlines would drive the bulk of the AI universe stocks up or down," the CIO said. "I don't think we're going to see that kind of uniformity going forward."As it stands now, action in the AI trade appears to be more of a "reality check" than a "full-blown unraveling," according to Wells Fargo Investment Institute's Sameer Samana. But he still believes there may be more pressure in the days and maybe even weeks ahead. "We recently downgrade[d] tech because we thought expectations had gotten too optimistic, and while the recent selling has taken some of that optimism out of the equation, we don't think it's fully done and may last through the midterms given the politicization of AI/data centers," the Wells Fargo head of global equities and real assets told CNBC.

title: Anthropic is AI trade's last big hope for a major IPO this year
description: A SpaceX advertisement on a digital billboard in Times Square celebrates the launch of SpaceX's initial public offering in New York on June 12, 2026.A
body: A SpaceX advertisement on a digital billboard in Times Square celebrates the launch of SpaceX's initial public offering in New York on June 12, 2026.Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty ImagesHeading into 2026, investors were excited at the prospect of a host of new initial public offerings, including ones from mega-cap private companies like SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI. But now investors will have to settle for less than they expected at the start of the year, with OpenAI ruling out its debut on the public markets in 2026 and several other planned offerings postponed this year. On prediction market platform Kalshi, speculators think the only major company left that might officially announce an IPO this year is Anthropic, which confidentially filed a prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in early June. The market on Kalshi asks traders if they think a series of companies will officially announce an IPO in 2026. The question of what constitutes an official announcement is resolved by the SEC declaring a company's S-1 effective, an IPO pricing or an exchange assigning a ticker to the stock. Contracts are resolved using various news outlets as sources. Of the 23 companies that Kalshi lists on its market that remain open to trade, only Anthropic offers greater than 50% odds — 75% as of Monday morning — to officially announce an IPO this year. Traders in January gave financial technology company Plaid 50% odds to debut on the public markets this year. They now place just a 10% chance the company, reportedly valued at $8 billion in the private market, goes public. Human resources and payroll platform Deel had 50-50 odds as recently as February, but now speculators see only a 3% chance the company goes public in 2026. Cloud and artificial intelligence platform Databricks' odds are just 1%, after seeing more than 50% odds in January. Similarly, OpenAI — Anthropic's chief rival — has just a 3% chance of going public after CEO Sam Altman said last month it didn't make sense to go public amid concerns over AI safety. Traders on Kalshi carry just 50-50 odds OpenAI makes an official IPO announcement by June 2027. Growing postponements IPO postponements, from across sectors, have grown in recent weeks. And while IPO proceeds this year are up sharply, driven by mega-cap debuts, notably SpaceX in June, the number of U.S. IPOs priced this year is actually down 33% compared with 2025, according to Renaissance Capital. Investors are betting on major AI companies, as well as those whose products are contributing to the AI build-out, to move from private to public markets as they seek larger pools of capital to finance development. Many have grown at a blistering pace, and public markets are seen as the next step to support that growth. Optimistic growth assumptions were called into question last week, however, when Anthropic revealed its revenue totaled $16.8 billion in the third quarter, weaker quarter-over-quarter growth than in past periods. "More questions than answers emerged around the reasons for revenue growth deceleration in September and whether Anthropic can grow revenue at the rate the market is expecting given dynamics such as [large language model] pricing pressure," wrote 22V Research analyst Dauvin Peterson on Sunday. "At the end of the day, the revised IPO valuation range starting at $1.5T vs the prior expectation of at least $2T was viewed as disappointing and added fuel to the fire for the AI-related equities that were already under pressure."Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Anthropic is AI trade's last big hope for a major IPO this year

title: Trump says he'd meet with Putin and Xi, criticizes Zelenskyy
description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on Oct. 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesPresident D
body: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters as he departs the White House on Oct. 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump said Monday that he would meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss how to end the Ukraine war, while ramping up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Trump suggested that a meeting between the world leaders, which Putin reportedly proposed, could take place without Zelenskyy present."Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump told reporters when asked about the potential meeting as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.The comments came as tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy have steadily risen in recent weeks, while Russia — which invaded Ukraine in 2022 — has received multiple breaks from the U.S.Trump had initially suggested that he would be more interested in discussing "denuclearization" with Putin and Xi, saying, "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."The Wall Street Journal had reported that Putin in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump floated the idea of a trilateral summit with Xi next month.That meeting could take place at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, which is set for Nov. 18 and Nov. 19, the Journal reported."If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too. But yeah, I would do that," Trump said in Monday's remarks.He also said that Russia and China, which have both been accused of supporting Iran in its ongoing military efforts against the U.S., have done "very little" for Tehran. And when asked about Zelenskyy's criticism of Trump's recent decision to waive new sanctions against Russia — and his recent claim that Trump is on the wrong side of history — the U.S. president once again lashed out at the Ukrainian leader."Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said. "Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago.""I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine," Trump added, echoing his prior call for Kyiv to "get a new president."Zelenskyy says that Starlink and Starshield, the critical satellite services offered by Elon Musk's SpaceX, have recently been degraded, and that U.S. intelligence sharing has also been disrupted, leaving Ukraine without advance warning of Russian strikes.  "No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," Zelenskyy said earlier Monday after a call with bipartisan U.S. lawmakers from the House and Senate.Trump said outside the White House that he does not know who ordered the interruption to the Starlink service, "But I'd like to find out."Musk said last week that the U.S. government and Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the U.S. caused the interruption, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Zelenskyy to be "very careful about making statements like this that aren't true."Zelenskyy also once again criticized Trump's decision to waive key provisions of a new Russian sanctions bill, which was signed last month after passing Congress with broad bipartisan support.He said he showed the lawmakers photos from the scene of a Russian attack in the Kharkiv region that killed six people, including a mother and her 1-year-old child."This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the easing of pressure," Zelenskyy said.Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a joint statement after the meeting, "Funding Russia's war machine, disabling Ukraine's satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace.""Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties," the senators said.Trump had already been criticized by members of both parties after announcing a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel on the global market, despite existing sanctions.But in Monday's remarks, Trump pushed back, saying he is "not looking to break up negotiations" with Putin on deals pertaining to Ukraine, Iran, diesel and the release of hostages.

schema.headline: Trump says he'd meet with Putin and Xi, criticizes Zelenskyy

title: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop
description: Apple CEO John Ternus during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Ima
body: Apple CEO John Ternus during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesApple announced a product launch event on Oct. 28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles." The email says "Pro and tell," suggesting the launch will focus on high-end "Pro" devices with powerful homegrown chips. Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall. He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.Apple's invite to media for the event. AppleIt will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.Apple updated its Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktops with new chips in August, and refreshed its MacBook Pro in the spring, along with a new low-cost MacBook Neo. But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024. In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones. Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors. Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500. Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. WATCH: Apple and Meta find new common ground in AIwatch now

title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
description: Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (C), alongside US President Donald Trump (R) and Social Security Administration commissioner Frank Bisignano (L),
body: Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (C), alongside US President Donald Trump (R) and Social Security Administration commissioner Frank Bisignano (L), speaks about "Trump accounts," investment savings accounts for children, in the Oval Office in the White House in Washington, DC on October 7, 2026. Alex Wroblewski | Afp | Getty ImagesU.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine. U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations. In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed. Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims. "President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press." "President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added. Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown."Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal. Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA. Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high. Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress."Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

schema.headline: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink

title: Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom
description: watch nowSaudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and dro
body: watch nowSaudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks. The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. "We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon," the conference organizers said in a statement. The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured. Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Citigroup's Jane Fraser.CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh. This screen grab taken from CCTV footage played on a screen during a press conference by the Saudi-led coalition in Riyadh on October 15, 2026, and made available via AFPTV, shows what the coalition says was a Houthi attack on Abha International Airport on October 7, 2026. - | Afp | Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference  has played a key part in Riyadh's plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017. The decision to postpone the conference underscores the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East as the U.S-Iran war spreads across the region. Houthi militants have launched repeated waves of missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia since the deadly airport attack earlier this month. The Houthis claimed on Monday to have attacked King Khalid International Airport again; Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to Yemen; Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea Coast; the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi naval forces.The Saudi military destroyed several drones launched at the Riyadh region on Friday and Saturday, a spokesperson for the kingdom's armed forces said. Missiles launched over the Red Sea were also intercepted Friday including one heading toward the port city and oil terminal Yanbu, the spokesperson said.

title: Gartner analyst behind tech rout: AI returns are not yet large enough to justify neocloud build-out
description: watch nowWall Street research and advisory firm Gartner is standing by its forecast that $3.5 trillion in AI investment could be on the rocks due to p
body: watch nowWall Street research and advisory firm Gartner is standing by its forecast that $3.5 trillion in AI investment could be on the rocks due to profitability concerns among the top AI models.Gartner's forecast, issued last week, helped send shockwaves through the AI trade. The firm's chief forecaster, John Lovelock, told CNBC Monday that returns are not yet backing up the full scale of investment. Consolidation and takeovers among AI-dedicated companies known as neoclouds could ensue, due partly to a mismatch in timing, he added."At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," he told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."That duopoly for the main commercial frontier models consists of Anthropic and OpenAI. The computing-power asset base that's being constructed by neoclouds to serve that duopoly requires a degree of cash flow for those businesses that isn't yet scaling in proportion to the investment, Lovelock said.Neoclouds would not be going out of business en masse, Lovelock reiterated, but could be subject to consolidation, such as takeovers and mergers. As a result of their profitability analysis, Gartner predicted last week that 80% of neoclouds, which are AI-dedicated computing power providers, could cease functioning as independent companies.Neoclouds were hit hard last week, helping to pull the rest of the stock market down with them.CoreWeave dropped 25%; Nebius dropped 25%; and IREN fell 16%. The S&P 500 finished down 2% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 4% for the week ending Oct. 16, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average finished up 0.7% as investors rotated away from technology stocks.CoreWeave was up about 2% in midday trading on Monday, while Nebius was up 3.3% and IREN was ahead 5.6%.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave 5 day.Analysts for Wolfe said in a Sunday note that the Gartner report likely contributed to the market stress."By the end of [Wednesday], the market appeared to already be on edge when a report from Gartner dropped, warning that more than $3.5tn in AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment by 2030, with neocloud providers particularly vulnerable," Stephanie Wolfe at Roth wrote to clients. Lovelock also said Monday that AI is a technology as opposed to a market, comparing it to table salt that will be sprinkled into existing commercial operations rather than creating an inherently new field in which companies will sell differentiated and competing products.In their Wednesday report, Gartner researchers found that overall "AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030.The finding came as revenue growth for frontier algorithm company Anthropic decelerated, falling from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% growth in the third. The quarterly revenue level of $16.8 billion for Anthropic, which many tech analysts view as one of the linchpins of the AI trade, is quite small relative to the more than $5 trillion that hyperscalers are expected to invest through 2030, the pace of which is increasing.OpenAI annual revenue expectations missed by $20 billion the week before, Roth at Wolfe noted.Gartner hasn't been alone in warning that investors' math for the AI buildout may be off. Jefferies' global head of equity strategy Chris Wood has been warning about capital destruction in AI since at least September. Famous investor Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC last week that macroeconomic considerations would lead to a challenging year for the stock market in 2027."[If] we sum up all the buybacks, M&A, all the positive things that have powered this market so much … say since 2009, if I sum up all those and then I subtract from that the IPOs, secondaries, unlocks, et cetera, then you've got certainly the most negative flow picture since 2009," he said.

schema.headline: Gartner analyst behind tech rout: AI returns are not yet large enough to justify neocloud build-out

title: Putin reportedly proposes three-way summit with Trump and Xi on Ukraine war — without Zelenskyy
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinpi
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report. The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel on the global market.U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters. "The president is open to anything that he can do to help bring a war to an end, if it's possible, and we'll continue to look for opportunities to do that," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.It comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. Over the past week, a series of moves by the Trump administration has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. It caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism from fellow Republicans.U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesOver the weekend, Trump defended his decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well as an executive order on Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham. Trump and Zelenskyy have traded criticism over how to end the war in Ukraine, with Trump accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace, while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia risks prolonging the conflict. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."The tensions come as Russia launched another wave of overnight attacks on Ukraine, firing 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones across the country, according to Zelenskyy.In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy said the strikes damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities, leaving at least 550,000 households without power. He also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the missile attacks. Casualties were reported, while a medical clinic, school, metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.Mounting tensionsUkraine's First Deputy Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Monday that Kyiv still hoped to retain Washington's support despite the growing tensions.Asked whether the Trump administration was abandoning Ukraine and siding with Russia, Derkach said he did not believe the U.S. was abandoning Kyiv, but stressed that Ukraine hoped Washington would continue helping it or at least "stay in the middle.""That's most important for us actually, not to lose the support of the U.S.," he said.Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine's transport infrastructure, including road border crossings, railways and shipping routes, Derkach said.It comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up global diesel prices. Despite an "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Oct. 11, Russia continued striking Ukrainian infrastructure. Kyiv paused its attacks for three days before resuming them last Thursday, citing continued Russian strikes."America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday. On Sunday, he also told Bloomberg that "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate.""I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukraine launching a strike of over 1,000 drones into Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St. Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.Starlink restrictions and intelligence sharingLast week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink. Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."Trump denied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces, after Reuters reported on Thursday that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from someone inside the White House, citing two U.S. officials.Read more of CNBC's Russia-Ukraine coverage:Trump's Russia diesel deal may offer Putin more than money — and spell trouble for UkraineZelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s energy ceasefire as drone attacks continueTrump declares ‘energy ceasefire’ between Russia and Ukraine; Zelenskyy is waiting for detailsUkraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machinePutin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy warns Russia preparing to deploy 10,000 North Korean troopsRussia ‘truly’ appreciates U.S. invite to G20 summit — but hasn’t decided if Putin will goZelenskyy says Ukraine ready for ‘energy ceasefire,’ calls for trilateral meeting with Putin, TrumpPutin floats ‘chance’ at peace with Ukraine as NATO chief warns Russia is becoming ‘increasingly reckless’Russia preparing ‘massive strikes’ on Ukraine’s energy sites after deadliest attack of the yearRussia's economy has defied the skeptics. Cracks are getting harder to hide'Winter is coming’: Ukraine fears its toughest test since Russia’s full-scale invasionThe Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.Additionally, Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that intelligence sharing between the two countries had been interrupted, but later "de-blocked."Rubio on Monday denied that Washington had suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contradicting Zelenskyy's claim that the flow of information had been briefly interrupted, Reuters reported.Speaking to reporters in Uzbekistan, Rubio insisted there had been no pause and said Zelenskyy should instead focus on ending the war, marking another public disagreement between Washington and Kyiv amid deteriorating relations.— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

title: In pictures: More than 500,000 took to the streets as France protests erupted into violence
description: watch nowProtests in France against rising living costs and declining public services turned violent over the weekend, with more than 500,000 people t
body: watch nowProtests in France against rising living costs and declining public services turned violent over the weekend, with more than 500,000 people taking to the streets.Hundreds of thousands of people marched through various cities and protested peacefully but others set fire to the city hall in Limoges, gutting the 19th-century building.Lyon's city tourist office was also set ablaze, supermarkets were looted and there were attacks on police officers and vehicles and luxury boutiques, in what was described as the country's worst unrest in years.Officers used tear gas to restrain the crowds. One protester died of a heart attack, and another lost a hand."Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," French President Emmanuel Macron said in a televised address to the nation on Sunday. He blamed "unrestrained violence" on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals."The demonstrations began last month as high school students across Paris lamented poor school conditions, including teacher shortages and unsatisfactory facilities. The demonstrations evolved into a nationwide protest. Protesters march through central Paris amid fires, smoke, police deployments and clashes during nationwide demonstrations against the high cost of living, on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France. title: Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments
description: The head of JPMorgan Chase's new security and resiliency initiative, Todd Combs, then portfolio manager at Berkshire Hathaway Inc., is seen at Berkshi
body: The head of JPMorgan Chase's new security and resiliency initiative, Todd Combs, then portfolio manager at Berkshire Hathaway Inc., is seen at Berkshire Hathaway's shareholders meeting in Omaha, Nebraska, May 4, 2014.Daniel Acker / Bloomberg / Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms.The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview. Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments, has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added. Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago.He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors, in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon.The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries. Troy Rohrbaugh and Douglas Petno, co-CEOs of Commercial & Investment Bank at JPMorganChase.Courtesy: JPMorganChase"There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said. These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said. In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup's founder.That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers."Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday. "Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said.Risky business?  JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor.Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago.In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank.That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine, a former co-head of investment banking. JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada.Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government's needs, he said. watch now

title: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
description: LONDON, ENGLAND - JULY 7: Deputy Governor for Financial Stability, Sarah Breeden, attends the Bank of England financial stability report press confere
body: LONDON, ENGLAND - JULY 7: Deputy Governor for Financial Stability, Sarah Breeden, attends the Bank of England financial stability report press conference at Bank Of England on July 7, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Doug Peters - WPA Pool/Getty Images)Wpa Pool | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesHedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday.Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress.watch now"One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an interview Thursday."It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was."Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconU.S. 10-Year Treasurys.Hedge fund assets swellWith gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday.  In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency.But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil. That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF. "The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said.Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market — particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt. Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19. Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-Year OATs.Earlier this month, 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on 10-year U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs.Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about the country's fiscal outlook — fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.

schema.headline: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely

title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan held without bail after Saudi government offers to pay
description: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. De
body: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeThe Saudi national accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters was ordered detained without bail pending trial Monday by a San Francisco federal judge who said that there is a "significant" risk he would flee.The order came at a court hearing where Judge Alex Tse sharply questioned the value of an offer by the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles to pay the full bail for Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who was working for OpenAI as an engineer when he allegedly planted the device in a television on Sept. 28.Tse said he found the Saudi offer "problematic.""It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out," Tse said in the courtroom, as Alfozan and several dozen of his supporters looked on."The Saudi government is saying, 'We'll take care of everything, we'll have supervision, we will pay the bond, we're not going to approve any travel documents.'" Tse noted. "But what confidence do I have that they're going to protect the interests of the [U.S.] government?""That he's not going to flee? He doesn't have to go all the way to Saudi Arabia," the judge said. "He just has to go to Canada or Mexico ... I don't see how that is in his favor."Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the United States, which the judge referred to at the hearing. Tse also noted that OpenAI has terminated Alfozan.Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted.Tse ordered Alfozan to return to court on Nov. 6.Prosecutors from the San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office during Monday's hearing, and in a detention memo, detailed Alfozan's ties to Saudi Arabia as they argued he was a flight risk. Those ties include his wife and their 3-month-old son, who left the United States shortly after his arrest.Prosecutors in that court filing Sunday said that Alfozan's alleged bugging of the artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."The filing says, "OpenAI executives met with government officials" in the company's San Francisco headquarters in the same conference room on days close to when it is alleged Alfozan planted the device."This is an ongoing investigation that may yet result in more serious charges," the filing says.Source: U.S. District Court in San Francisco, U.S. v. Alfozan.Prosecutors said in the filing that Alfozan has access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said. "He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.Prosecutors in their filing said Alfozan had been "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026.Alfozan communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, prosecutors said.Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say how Alfozan knew that person. "Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing says."In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote. "The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."The filing does not say the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from the AI giant.Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined Raed as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.The recording device planted at OpenAI's office, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeProsecutors in the same filing said the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their baby son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12. The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said. Alfozan's lawyer, William Perchik, told Judge Tse that the defendant was willing to put up $1 million in assets to secure his release, in addition to the Saudi Consulate's offer. A letter from the consulate was included in a motion for pretrial release by Perchik.Pernik had asked Tse to release Alfozan on bail with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13.Pernik, in arguing for Alfozan's release, said the defendant has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit-participating units, his lawyer said in a court filing.Prosecutors in their detention memo said Alfozan had planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12."On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing by prosecutors said.The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.The filing also says that after Alfozan's arrest, his iPhone was found to contain photographs dated Sept. 22 to 28 depicting "at least one additional concealed device as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred.""The defendant's residence contained several electronic components similar to those in thecustomized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room," the filing said.OpenAI also found another recording device in a bag Alfozan inadvertently left behind in a printer room on Oct. 5, the same day he was seen on camera checking behind the TV where the first recording device had been left in the conference room, prosecutors have said. The camera was installed after OpenAI discovered the recording device on Sept. 30, prosecutors said.His cellphone also contained a deleted note from September "with links to various recording devices, including devices made by Seeed Studio, the manufacturer of the devices OpenAI found in its offices and the devices FBI agents found in the defendant's residence," the filing said.Another note, entitled "OpenAI leave," suggests that Alfozan planned early pickup "of the devices he had installed or intended to install and then extending his planned parental 'leave to full,'" the filing said.In addition to being in contact with a Saudi royal, Alfozan "was pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including participating in the Misk Foundation's '2030 Leaders' program, which would have required his in- person participation in Riyadh," prosecutors said.A day before she left the U.S. with their baby, Alfozan's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her U.S. visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia — and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same," the filing said.Alfozan's lawyer, Pernik, in his request that Alfozan be released into home detention, said, "nationality is not evidence of flight," and that his planned travel to Saudi Arabia was for "family and immigration reasons." Alfozan's wife's 60-day post-employment grace period for her own visa was expiring on Oct. 12, the originally scheduled date of their flight, the lawyer said."Mr. Alfozan was made aware of OpenAI finding the device per its own filings and OpenAI'spublic statements, approximately eight to ten days before he was arrested," Pernik wrote. "If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time."The lawyer also said that Alfozan, who had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia for himself and his family, regularly bought one-way tickets because he has learned they are more cost-effective than changing his flights at the last minute.Pernik also wrote that the Saudi Consulate General confirmed in writing to the U.S. Pretrial Services Office on Thursday that it "'will not issue any travel documents' to Mr. Alfozan during his release and that, if he requests one, it 'undertakes to promptly notify U.S. Pretrial Services.'"The attorney argued that prosecutors have not shown that Alfozan is a serious flight risk."Mr. Alfozan has lived in the United States for fifteen years and in the Bay Area for roughly ten," Pernik wrote. "Fifty-four people, at least twenty-seven of them in the Bay Area, have written to the Court, and they describe someone who organizes dinners, welcomes newcomers, mentors students, and shows up for friends' weddings, birthdays, and moves.""That is not the profile of a person with one foot out the door," Pernik said.— Jordan Novet reported from San Francisco.

schema.headline: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan held without bail after Saudi government offers to pay

title: Cornell sexual assault case has some prospective students rethinking plans, consultants say
description: Students walk on the campus of Cornell University on Sept. 30, 2026, in Ithaca, New York.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesAs Cornell University faces scrut
body: Students walk on the campus of Cornell University on Sept. 30, 2026, in Ithaca, New York.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesAs Cornell University faces scrutiny over its handling of sexual assault allegations, some prospective students are reconsidering whether to apply, according to college admissions consultants who spoke with CNBC.The concerns come just weeks before Cornell's Nov. 1 early-decision deadline, when applicants must decide whether to submit an application under a binding agreement to attend the Ivy League university if admitted.Amid public outrage over the handling of the 2024 alleged incident and the ensuing Jane Doe lawsuit, some high school seniors have decided to take the school out of consideration, according to Christopher Rim, president and CEO of college consulting firm Command Education."I originally had nine students applying to Cornell, four were early — now we have zero applying early," he said.The lawsuit centers on a civil complaint filed in September by a former student identified as Jane Doe. She alleges that in October 2024 she was sexually assaulted at one of the school's fraternity houses on Cornell's campus in Ithaca, New York.Jamie Beaton, co-founder and CEO of college consulting firm Crimson Education, also said he is "seeing some Cornell applicants reconsider applying there based on campus safety and culture concerns." Read more CNBC personal finance coverageCNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approachTrump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donationsThousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher paymentsSocial Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Cornell directed CNBC to Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff's Oct. 13 message. In a statement, the university said it is conducting an independent review, led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, to examine long-standing policies and practices. Separately, Cornell suspended all fraternity parties and social events for the remainder of the 2026-27 academic year."These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now," Kotlikoff said in the statement. What comes next is key, Rim said. "It's very important for Cornell to make sure they do the right thing and make actual changes to their policies," he said. "Then they are going to have to convince students and families they are serious about it."Will Cornell's application numbers change?Changing course so close to the early-decision deadline can be difficult for applicants who have spent months tailoring their applications to a specific Cornell school, a distinctive part of the university's application process, according to Beaton.Some applicants "feel psychologically committed," he said, and are "staying the course, and are holding onto hope that the scrutiny on Cornell will force it to make serious reforms to institutional conduct and culture as a result of this."In some cases, applying early decision can improve an applicant's odds of admission but leaves less time to work on the application or compare options. The regular-decision deadline for Cornell is Jan. 2.watch nowGoing forward, "what we expect is that things will be loud in the short term," Beaton said, referring specifically to this application cycle. But he added that there will likely be minimal long-term movement in application volumes or yield, which is the percent of students who choose to enroll after being admitted."Scandals at highly selective universities don't move application volumes in a lasting way, since the pull of the brand, the outcomes and the network is too strong," Beaton said.Cornell is the largest Ivy by undergraduate enrollment. With an acceptance rate under 10%, Cornell most recently admitted 5,776 applicants to the Class of 2030, according to the university's independent student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun.

schema.headline: Cornell sexual assault case has some prospective students rethinking plans, consultants say

title: Elon Musk says he'll give a SpaceX share to every child in America next year
description: Key PointsSpaceX boss Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give one of his shares in the company to every child in the U.S. next year.That would amount to
body: Key PointsSpaceX boss Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give one of his shares in the company to every child in the U.S. next year.That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares. Musk did not provide further details on how the share giveaway would happen.watch nowSpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year. Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday."This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.CNBC has reached out to SpaceX and Musk's family office for further details.Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and Trump Accounts, praised the move and suggested in a post on X that the SpaceX shares could be distributed via Trump accounts. "Incredible Elon!" he wrote. "This will be the largest philanthropic gift in history! 70 M accounts - every citizen under 18 & every child born forevermore now has a free, lifetime investment acct making them an owner in the upside of America & our greatest companies!"Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions.The Tesla CEO has spent more than $276 million in donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election. The world's richest person poured $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever.Read more CNBC tech newsGoogle says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skepticalWomen may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show whyAnthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruptionAlways on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardyWhen it comes to fulfilling his philanthropic promises, Musk has a spotty track record. For example, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO contributed about $38 million to OpenAI, which he co-founded as a nonprofit research lab, between 2016 and 2020. But he had promised to contribute up to $1 billion, and cut off donations to the organization amid a battle with cofounders for control of the company.In 2021, Musk said he would donate $6 billion to the United Nations World Food Program if it could show him a plan for how they'd use the money to "solve world hunger." While the WFP posted a plan, Musk did not donate.Musk's foundation has also repeatedly fallen shy of making the minimum donations it's required to by law, and as The New York Times previously reported, its donations go to charities that closely benefit Musk and his companies directly.Musk's post came just after Anthropic revealed plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing.Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.— CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report.watch now

schema.headline: Elon Musk says he'll give a SpaceX share to every child in America next year
